cited_details.statement: Speech disorders affect articulation, fluency, voice, and language production across the lifespan, and aphasia represents one of the most studied post-stroke conditions (https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd000425.pub4).
Aphasia, an acquired language impairment following brain damage, affects approximately one third of individuals who experience a stroke (https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd000425.pub4).

Children with speech sound disorders (SSDs) likewise constitute a large proportion of speech-language therapists' caseloads, with intervention typically involving articulatory or phonologically based approaches (https://doi.org/10.1177/0265659014550420).

The clinical diversity of these conditions has motivated growing interest in AI-based automated tools that can supplement traditional therapy and reduce dependence on scarce clinical resources (https://doi.org/10.1177/0265659014550420).
Automatic speech recognition is a central enabling technology for these tools, underpinning both pronunciation evaluation and mispronunciation detection (https://aclanthology.org/W12-5808.pdf).

Modern self-supervised models such as wav2vec 2.0 demonstrated that representations learned from raw speech audio alone followed by fine-tuning on transcribed speech can outperform previous semi-supervised methods (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/wav2vec-2.0%3A-A-Framework-for-Self-Supervised-of-Baevski-Zhou/49a049dc85e2380dde80501a984878341dd8efdf).

Earlier work used ASR toolkits such as CMUSphinx, in which pronunciation evaluation and mispronunciation detection were performed using Sphinx trained on native and non-native exemplar pronunciations with adaptation techniques (https://aclanthology.org/W12-5808.pdf).

Hair and colleagues specifically evaluated ASR for child speech therapy applications, showing that ASR on disordered child speech with limited training data and mobile-device-friendly techniques can provide utterance feedback suitable for therapy apps (https://psi.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/hair2019evaluating.pdf).
Automated assessment tools have been developed for several disorder categories, with particular attention to childhood speech sound disorders (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884147/).

Shahin and colleagues designed an automated tool to assess productions from children with apraxia of speech, consisting of a clinician interface, a mobile application, and a speech processing engine (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167639315000382).

A 2017 study on automatic analysis of pronunciations for children with SSDs highlighted that Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) systems aim to help a child learn the correct pronunciations of words (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884147/).

The same review noted that there is no consensus among Speech-Language Therapists about which CAPT systems work reliably, with the prevailing assumption being that practicing with such programs is less reliable than traditional methods (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5884147/).

Benway and Preston (2023) prospectively validated motor-based intervention with automated mispronunciation detection of rhotics in residual SSDs, using GMM-HMM derived intervals fed into a PERCEPT-R classifier to predict clinician perceptual judgment of /ɹ/ (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).
The PERCEPT-R classifier specifically predicts clinician perceptual judgment of /ɹ/ productions, supporting biofeedback-driven intervention in residual SSDs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).

For Mandarin-speaking children, a deep-learning system has been described that analyzes acoustic data to assist in the diagnosis and classification of four distinct types of SSDs (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9324778/).
Fluency disorders have also been addressed by AI-based modeling (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01231).
Speech disorders such as stuttering disrupt the normal flow of speech, motivating the development of automated detection systems (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01231).

Das and colleagues proposed stuttering disfluency prediction using explainable attribution vectors derived from facial muscle movements, noting that stuttering has a prevalence of approximately 1% in adults and a lifetime incidence of about 5% (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01231).
Their approach emphasizes interpretability by attributing predictions to specific articulatory cues captured from video (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01231).
Mobile and home-based platforms have expanded the reach of these tools beyond the clinic (https://psi.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/hair2019evaluating.pdf).

A study of mobile speech therapy applications observed that the "Speech Therapy for Apraxia" app is suitable for children with apraxia and speech disorders, allowing users to select target phonemes (http://jmr.tums.ac.ir/index.php/jmr/article/download/133/80).
Mobile deployment of ASR for disordered child speech has been shown to be feasible with limited training data (https://psi.engr.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/hair2019evaluating.pdf).

A requirements analysis for tangible user interfaces and Internet of Things artefacts for children with SSDs emphasized that more research is needed and that a unified method or framework to address SSD intervention tools is currently lacking (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0949276b131c3d4b2ed993c167fdf13d2fa886d2).

This work combined a systematic literature review, focus group, and nationwide questionnaire to determine system requirements for home-based interventions, while also addressing data security and privacy issues (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0949276b131c3d4b2ed993c167fdf13d2fa886d2).
A persistent challenge in this field is the gap between laboratory accuracy and clinical effectiveness (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).
Because lab accuracy of clinical speech technology systems may be overoptimistic, clinical validation in real patient populations remains vital before deployment (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).

The Cochrane review of speech and language therapy for aphasia following stroke underscores that rigorous evidence is still needed to identify which patients benefit most from specific therapy approaches (https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd000425.pub4).
AI-based tools will need to incorporate similar evidence-based evaluation frameworks to demonstrate efficacy in everyday settings (https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd000425.pub4).
The GMM-HMM framework used for mispronunciation detection identifies phonetic intervals that can drive classifier feedback in real time (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).

In summary, AI-based automated speech therapy tools have progressed from rule-based and early ASR systems toward deep learning and self-supervised models, with applications spanning apraxia, aphasia, fluency, and pediatric SSDs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).
Continued prospective clinical validation in diverse populations will be essential for translating these tools into routine practice (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19090).
